newsitem.title: HUNGARY: EIB to increase lending to EU entry favourites.
newsitem.headline: EIB to increase lending to EU entry favourites.

text.p: The European Investment Bank (EIB) said it would step up lending for five east European countries earmarked for the first wave of European Union expansion, ahead of endorsement of the list by EU leaders.

"We will be accelerating our lending to what we call a pre-accession lending arrangement within the next few weeks," Chris Knowles, head of the EIB's central and eastern Europe lending operations told a news conference.

In a policy blueprint for the next century, the European Commission recommended this month that Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic, Slovenia and Estonia should be invited to accession talks -- along with Cyprus -- early next year. They may then become members in four to six years' time.
Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Romania and Bulgaria would have a separate status allowing them to prepare for membership at their own pace.
EU governments must endorse the list by December but differences have emerged as to whether the Commission's recommended list is final.

Italy, Denmark and Sweden told their EU partners during a televised debate last week that the distinction risked creating a new curtain between east and west, fuelling popular resentment and setting back the reform process in the countries left out.
Knowles said the EIB, the European Union's bank lending arm, was already working on the basis that the list will not be altered by governments.
"(The list) could change but I think it's a safe working assumption that it won't," he told Reuters.

Knowles was speaking after a new agreement was signed by Hungarian telecommunications company Matav Rt with an international bank consortium led by ABN-AMRO Bank on the issue of a five-year bank guarantee worth 168 million Ecus ($180.4 million).

The bank guarantee will replace the state guarantee for investment loans granted by the Luxembourg-based European Investment Bank (IEB) in 1990 and 1994, and is the first such release of state guarantees in Central Europe.
Knowles said new lending arrangements for favoured EU applicants would be comparable to those agreed with Spain, Portugal and Greece in the five years leading up to their accession to the EU.
"During that period lending increased several times," he said.

Knowles said the EIB had so far lent a total 872 million Ecu to Hungary, including almost 300 million to the banking sector, mainly to enable Hungarian banks to lend to companies, and the remainder for transport and municipal infrastructure.
He added that the releasing of state guarantees on the Matav loans was a recognition of the progress both the company and Hungary's economy had made.

"The move reflects the strong progress made by Matav before and after its privatisation and the increasingly favourable environment in which MATAV operates, that is, the strength of the Hungarian economy."

Matav is 67 percent owned by a 50-50 consortium of Deutsche Telekom and Ameritech Corp, while the state holds a 25 percent stake and the rest is held by a variety of investors. ($ = 0.931 European Currency Unit ECUs)
